articles.title: No agenda, no rush, no leaving San Francisco: Benchmark’s partners on investing in a frenzied market | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Benchmark may have grown its funds and swapped out some partners, but onstage the five who are left sounded like friends who just happen to be running one of the Valley’s most storied firms
articles.body_text: The players sometimes change. I sat down with four of Benchmark’s partners three years ago , and three of those individuals are no longer with the firm. The capital commitments have changed, too. This summer, Benchmark announced $2 billion across two funds, marking only the second time in its 31-year history that it has veered from raising a far smaller vehicle. But at this week’s TechCrunch Disrupt, the venture firm’s five partners convincingly portrayed a close-knit team that’s not about to put the pedal to the metal, even as many of their rivals do exactly that. The world may be speeding up, but they’re investing at the pace Benchmark always has: just two or three new bets per year per partner. The world is drowning in information, yet their Monday partner meetings still have no agenda. And while economic indicators point to trouble ahead, they don’t seem too bothered, seeing many of the warning signs as products of X-fueled hysteria. Here’s what Benchmark’s five general partners — gathered together on our stage — had to say at the show. Some of the comments below have been edited for length and clarity; you can watch the full interview at the end of the article. Benchmark has evolved in some ways, including a bigger core fund and a new growth fund. How do you think about adapting without losing what makes you Benchmark? Peter Fenton: The craft that hasn’t changed is the core fund: working closely with founders at the beginning. It’s usually a 10-to-15-year commitment, [working] shoulder to shoulder, and that doesn’t scale. There’s also been inflation. We held the core fund at $500 million for 20 years, and it has just inflated to be consistent with the existing economy, which we hadn’t done and that was probably a tactical error on our part. [As for the growth fund] it’s an expansion of our mandate. In some ways, we get permission from the ecosystem to do more than just the core early-stage business. [Not having this previously] was a fork in our eye. A number of opportunities that came to Benchmark would have returned somewhere between 10 and 1,000x to Benchmark, and we were constricted by our early-stage focus. Are you thinking to make handful of bets with that $1.25 billion growth fund? Fenton: We all have different answers, which is the beauty of a partnership. I’d love for us to have, as that great J.P. Morgan paper puts it, the agony and ecstasy of a concentrated portfolio. If the fund is successful, one or two investments will generate 90% of the returns. So I think it’s four to six, maybe seven to eight. Ev, you joined Benchmark late last year. You’ve worked at Founders Fund, Bond, and Kleiner Perkins. How does Benchmark differ? Ev Randall: Every firm is ultimately a collection of the people within the firm and how they work together. Some are very hierarchical, with a 50- or 60-person investment team and investment processes that are federated into product groups. And then you have small partnerships. Very early in my career, I was drawn to small partnerships because they allow a higher level of throughput and fidelity in your conversations, where you don’t feel like you’re making decisions through some Byzantine corporate structure. You’re going out on the field together, like a sports team. And then the other piece is: You have to find your people, You have to find people who you not only like but admire. With Benchmark, with the current crop of GPs, it was obvious that everyone liked each other and got along, but it went deeper than that. It’s a group that admires each other and learns from each other. That mix of attributes is very rare, and when I saw it, I immediately wanted to join, and I think Jack felt the same way also as a newcomer. Jack, you joined in February, but it was just a year ago that you raised a second, $275 million fund for your own firm in what you told the Wall Street Journal took one week. You have a hugely popular podcast. Why join Benchmark?

articles.title: Anthropic says it’s committing 5% of its shares to a ‘public benefit fund’ | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Anthropic said that it will commit 5% of its shares to the fund.
articles.body_text: Anthropic announced today that it’s creating a “public benefit fund” that will give the company “increased flexibility and scale” to support projects for societal good. Anthropic said that it will commit 5% of its shares to the fund — structured as a wholly-owned entity within the company — with the option to contribute an additional 2% for every 50% increase in Anthropic’s value. And it offered some broad-strokes ideas for how this money might actually be used, such as “large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.” There’s also the impact that AI might have on the job market, which Anthropic has already committed $200 million to study . But the company said, “Given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.” Anthropic’s announcement comes as the AI industry faces increasingly negative public sentiment, which CEO Dario Amodei has described as “fundamentally a crisis of trust.” If you’re wondering who will actually decide which public benefits are worth funding, Anthropic said it will share more information about structure and governance in the coming months. articles.title: Everyone’s watching the Elizabeth Holmes documentary ‘You Can See Everything’ | TechCrunch
articles.summary: "You Can See Everything" is having the second biggest opening weekend ever for a documentary film.
articles.body_text: “You Can See Everything” is already a box office sensation, with a $15 million opening weekend (based on Sunday estimates). That’s the second biggest opening weekend ever for a documentary film. The nearly three-hour movie — first revealed last month at a secretive screening at the Telluride Film Festival — is only playing in 855 theaters this weekend. (In contrast, the weekend’s number one movie, “Street Fighter,” is playing in 3,575.) But it had a reported 2,000 sellout screenings, and the reviews are overwhelmingly positive; “You Can See Everything” currently has a score of 99% on both Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic . The story of Elizabeth Holmes’ rise and fall — founding blood-testing startup Theranos, attracting support from many of Silicon Valley’s biggest names, then ultimately being sentenced to 11 years in prison for defrauding investors — has already been told in books, podcasts, TV shows, and other documentaries. But “You Can See Everything”’s filmmakers were given extensive access to Holmes and her family in the month before she went to jail, and the involvement of “The Rehearsal” creator Nathan Fielder — who co-directed the film with Lance Oppenheim — made the whole thing even more intriguing. While I haven’t seen the movie myself, I can at least attest to the difficulty of finding tickets in Manhattan: I spent a good chunk of yesterday trying to find a screening for tonight, and I found exactly one with seats available that weren’t in the front row. (Yes, of course I’m going.) TechCrunch’s Amanda Silberling already got to see it on Thursday . She wrote that the enigmatic Holmes finally seems to have met her match in Fielder, a deadpan comedian who’s arguably just as strange and mysterious as she is. Fielder’s month with Holmes is apparently just the beginning of what sounds like an increasingly surreal, metatextual odyssey. The discussion around “You Can See Everything” may be making it harder for other tech-centric films to break through. Aaron Sorkin’s “Social Network” follow-up “The Social Reckoning” opened to a disappointing $5.5 million last weekend , and has already fallen entirely out of the top 10. And Alex Gibney’s four-hour documentary “Musk” — hampered, perhaps, by resistance from social platforms and a four-hour runtime — made only $306,702 this weekend. articles.body_text: After chatbot startup Character.AI filed for bankruptcy earlier this week, many of its employees will have the opportunity to take jobs at Disney. Character.AI’s former CEO Karandeep Anand recently became the entertainment giant’s first CTO , and the startup previously said that Disney had agreed to acquire some of its assets for $20 million. A legal filing spotted by Bloomberg revealed more details about the agreement between Character.AI and Disney, with Disney agreeing to make employment offers to at least 60 Character.AI employees — the majority of the workforce — paying them an estimated $60 million in annual compensation. The filing says that despite its “large and engaged user base,” Character.AI has been hobbled by high costs and “potential litigation-related liabilities and regulatory engagement.” (The company was sued by the mother of a 14-year-old boy who said her son became obsessed with one of Character.AI’s chatbots before committing suicide; it also faces government investigations over child safety concerns .) articles.summary: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it.
articles.body_text: As I wrapped my TechCrunch Disrupt interview with Rivian CEO and founder RJ Scaringe , I kept circling back to one question: What does Scaringe want Rivian to become? If you look at Rivian’s moves over the past year, it’s clear that Scaringe wants the company to be much more than an EV maker. But he doesn’t want to stray completely from that mission either. Rivian is far more vertically integrated than it was just a couple of years ago. It has developed its own AI models to power its in-vehicle assistant and is building an end-to-end automated driving stack for its passenger vehicles and future robotaxis through a partnership with Uber. It’s even developing custom silicon , a 5 nm processor in collaboration with Arm and TSMC. And then there is its $5.8 billion joint technology venture with VW Group focused on electric architecture and software. Scaringe’s ambitions extend beyond Rivian as well, although there is always a link back. He created a micromobility skunkworks program that has since spun out into a startup called Also. And he founded an industrial robotics startup called Mind Robotics, which is now 31% owned by Rivian and counts the automaker as a prospective customer. (Scaringe announced onstage that former Ford, Apple, and Tesla executive Doug Field has been hired as president of Mind Robotics.) Scaringe’s aspirations were on display as he talked of not only expanding the joint venture with VW to cover AI and autonomy, but also licensing Rivian’s tech to “many different brands.” So what does Rivian look like at the end of the decade? Certainly not just a maker of electric trucks and SUVs. The term I kept coming back to was “tech supplier.” Hear me out. Rivian is clearing a path toward licensing its electric architecture and software as well as its AI models and autonomy stack. Meanwhile, the Mind Robotics startup it partially owns is building industrial robots to not only be used in Rivian factories, but also sold to other companies. Then there’s the robotaxi business. A successful launch with Uber could open the door to more deals. And Scaringe is already imagining how autonomy could reshape Rivian’s own vehicles. “Where it gets really interesting is then you think beyond R2 and R3 and start to imagine the form factors that you want to build for a personally owned autonomous vehicle. You know, it opens up all kinds of design opportunities. It can create dramatically different experiences,” he said in an interview with TechCrunch. “I’m wildly excited about what the next 10 years look like in transportation because of what this enables us to dream and think about.” Bedrock Robotics , a startup developing autonomous driving tech for construction vehicles, is raising $600 million , Axios reported, citing sources. Dot Ai completed its acquisition of electric vehicle car-sharing business Envoy Technologies in a $65 million all-stock transaction, according to a regulatory filing . Evos , a startup that developed AI agents to automate work for industrial businesses, including freight brokerages, raised $9 million in a pre-seed round co-led by Uncork Capital and Field Ventures. Mana Battery, a Colorado-based startup developing anode-free sodium batteries, raised $10.15 million in a round led by Voyager Ventures.

articles.title: TikTok permanently bans ‘Musk’ documentary advertising account | TechCrunch
articles.summary: A four-hour documentary about Elon Musk continues to meet resistance from social media platforms.
articles.body_text: A four-hour documentary about Elon Musk continues to meet resistance from social media platforms, with TikTok banning the film’s advertising account. According to a story in The Hollywood Reporter , the documentary’s distributor Bleecker Street was recently notified by TikTok that the account had received a “permanent suspension” due to its political content. TechCrunch has reached out to TikTok for comment. Ads promoting the trailer for “Musk” — directed by Oscar-winner filmmaker Alex Gibney — were initially rejected by Meta and YouTube as well , though those platforms eventually allowed the ad, with Meta blaming the rejection on “an error.” Gibney recently confirmed that the film’s international distributor Universal had wavered in its plans to release “Musk,” though it’s now moving forward. X, which Musk owns, has refused to carry ads for “Musk.” TikTok’s U.S. operations are partly owned by Larry Ellison — who, like Musk, has been a notable supporter of President Donald Trump. “Musk” opened in just four theaters last weekend and is now rolling out more broadly. Next year, it’s supposed to stream on HBO — now part of Paramount/Skydance and led by Ellison’s son David . articles.title: Anthropic says its workforce has become less junior and is spending more time in meetings | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The composition of Anthropic’s workforce and the type of work getting done have changed significantly in the past year.
articles.body_text: The composition of Anthropic’s workforce and the type of work getting done have changed significantly in the past year, according to a report that the AI company published on Friday. Anthropic argues that its own workplace trends could be indicators of “how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy,” especially since the company “has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI.” But even if other organizations never embrace AI as thoroughly or in the exact same way as Anthropic, the report offers an intriguing glimpse at how the company currently operates. Notably, Anthropic is making fewer junior hires, with the proportion of junior-level employees in technical departments falling from 21% to 14% since early 2025, and the proportion of junior technical hires falling even more sharply, from 27% to 9%. Anthropic also says that technical teams now represent a smaller share of the overall workforce, falling from 61% to 56% — a trend that it attributes to “natural expansion of business functions as the company scales,” as well as “coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves.” One employee reportedly described an “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything.” In an April 2026 survey, 27% of employees said they had become more productive because of Claude and 20% said their job had shifted “from actually doing work to managing Claudes”; apparently one engineer compared this to babysitting: “When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.” In fact, the report suggests “human attention and judgement” are becoming a “bottleneck” for productivity, as Claude produces a “deluge” of text that needs to be read and organized. Unsurprisingly, the report argues that AI adoption has made the company more productive, as indicated by “more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts.” The company acknowledges that “more code does not necessarily mean better code or business impact,” but it also hasn’t found any indications that code quality is declining. The report says that based on calendar data, meeting time per employee is up 20% compared to a year ago, and it’s up 16% for technical contributors. The company attributes this to the importance of “human trust and accountability,” with employees repeatedly describing “face-to-face coordination as indispensable.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . articles.title: Replit makes OpenAI its default over Anthropic, CEO says | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Over the weekend, Masad clarified that OpenAI would replace Anthropic as its default model provider. Claude will still be available to customers on the platform.
articles.body_text: Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt . Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer partnering with Anthropic. “I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.” It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser. After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default. This shift could significantly reduce Replit’s spend with Anthropic since most customers stick with the default rather than selecting a model themselves. Prior to striking a deal with OpenAI, Replit relied on Anthropic’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted on stage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s. “Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models…OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.” Masad’s comments on stage were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place. There is evidence on the company’s website , blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was promoting Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities. Masad also shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue. “We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.” Backstage, Masad told TechCrunch that he expects more than half of Replit’s revenue to come from enterprise and government customers in 2027.

articles.title: Ember’s new temperature-controlled mug makes my nightly tea ritual even better | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The biggest change about Ember's new mug is that you no longer have to open the app to adjust your drink’s temperature.
articles.body_text: With the nights getting chillier, I’ve been reaching for a cup of tea more often. And if there’s one thing that can make a cozy fall night even better, it’s a warm drink that actually stays warm. Enter Ember’s new Mug 3 , the latest version of the company’s temperature-controlled smart mug, which is designed to keep your drink at just the right temperature for as long as you sip. Ember first introduced its smart mug in 2016 to solve a problem most coffee and tea drinkers know all too well: getting distracted for a few minutes, only to return to a lukewarm drink. Now, the company is back with its third-generation mug, which brings a handful of practical upgrades. The biggest change is that you no longer have to open the app to adjust your drink’s temperature. Instead, you can use the button on the bottom of the mug to cycle through five preset temperatures, starting at 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Each press raises the temperature by five degrees, up to a maximum of 145 degrees, so you can easily make your drink a little hotter with each click. Honestly, this is the feature I ended up using the most during my time testing out the mug. At night, when I’m curled up in bed with a book and a cup of tea, my phone is usually somewhere across the room. Being able to adjust my drink without getting up to find it is a small convenience, but one I genuinely appreciate. It’s also a welcome change for users who have reported running into connectivity or pairing issues with the Ember app. That said, I do have one complaint: the button is located on the bottom of the mug. It’s a peculiar design choice when you’re dealing with a cup full of hot liquid, and it isn’t particularly easy to press, either. I often found myself tilting the mug and pressing down firmly to get it to respond. So, while I appreciate the addition of on-mug controls, I wish Ember had made the button easier to reach. If you prefer using your phone, the Ember app still offers plenty of customization. After pairing the mug with your phone over Bluetooth, you can choose presets based on what you’re drinking. Ember recommends 136 degrees Fahrenheit for black coffee, 132 degrees for green tea, and 142 degrees for lemon water. You can also create your own temperature presets, which is handy if you like your drinks a little hotter or cooler than the recommended settings. The Mug 3 also comes with a few other upgrades, including a sliding lid designed to help prevent spills. The mug can also keep your drink at its desired temperature for up to three hours on a single charge. And it’s the first mug in Ember’s lineup to be top-rack dishwasher-safe, making cleanup easier. (Just keep in mind that it isn’t microwave-safe.) The Ember Mug 3 comes in two sizes: a 10-ounce model for $129 and a 14-ounce version for $149. The smaller mug is available in black, white, and stainless steel, while the larger size comes in eight colors, including sage green, lavender, powder blue, salt blue, sandstone, white, black, and matcha green. Alongside the new mug, Ember also introduced the Tumbler 2 , which replaces both the Travel Mug 2 and the original Tumbler in its lineup. The 16-ounce tumbler features a slimmer, taller design intended to fit standard car cup holders. It’s available in black for $179, while the Travel Mug 2 will remain available until supplies run out. The products are available to purchase on Ember’s website, Target, and Amazon.

articles.title: Mark Wahlberg wants to take on the longevity-startup crowd with an affordable gym concept | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Mark Wahlberg, who once sank money into a gym chain that got kicked off the NYSE, is now building his own, and he promises you’ll get a cold plunge, a blood panel and a protein muffin without needing a trust fund.
articles.body_text: Mark Wahlberg has started companies of his own and backed plenty of others. But he says the gym he’s opening in December has him more excited than anything he’s done in his entire career. It also goes after a corner of the market where venture money keeps flowing: pricey, diagnostics-heavy wellness. Speaking with us at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco on Thursday, the actor said the first Municipal Gym opens in December. It’s a 32,000-square-foot club outside Las Vegas with blood work, epigenetic testing, recovery gear, compression therapy, cold plunges, and a café that serves up protein muffins, among other things. He’s pitching it as the affordable alternative to the longevity clubs that charge tens of thousands of dollars a year for much the same thing. It’s the second part of a scheme that was, in some ways, first hatched seven years ago with a casual sportswear line. The clothing brand Municipal launched during COVID, which Wahlberg freely volunteered “was not a good idea,” given that clothing was a lousy business to enter in 2020, with retailers from J.Crew to Brooks Brothers going bankrupt. It grew out of what he’d been seeing as a celebrity fitness spokesperson. He’d done collabs with various brands, and other companies kept approaching him to be their brand ambassador, but they all seemed to want the same thing, he said. “Everybody just kind of wanted to sell T-shirts and sneakers. And I was like, well, I want to kind of have a bigger impact on people’s lives as a whole.” By that, he meant what people eat, what supplements they take, how they train, and how they recover. “We figured, okay, we’ll start in the apparel space, and then we’ll build from there.” He says he only takes swings at “things that I’m very passionate about and things that are a direct extension of who I am.” Even without a pandemic, clothing is a brutal business, as we pointed out, citing Lululemon’s repeated quality-control challenges . But Wahlberg didn’t seem fazed, talking instead about why the gym fits his vision. He thought it “always could be great for the brand” in part because it gives people a place to “actually feel and touch the clothes” before they buy. Besides, he continued, how people exercise is “another big part of people’s lives.” Most in the space have been laser-focused on the high end. Fountain Life, the longevity company co-founded by Tony Robbins, raised $18 million last year to expand its centers for wealthy clients, and a full subscription runs $21,500 a year, according to reports. The Estate, a company co-founded by Robbins and hospitality executive Sam Nazarian, is still mapping out plans to charge $35,000 memberships to its wellness centers. Equinox is similarly building a waitlist for a $36,000 longevity add-on that it plans to launch atop a traditional gym membership. Wahlberg says Municipal aims for that same luxury tier but for a lot less. “We have a better price point than our competitors, and we’re going to get far more results,” he said. For $99, he said as an example, members will receive three rounds of blood work and an hour with a doctor to flag what they’re predisposed to. Supplements and hormone therapy are also “right there.” When we asked whether the gyms will double as storefronts for his other products (he owns a supplements brand , for example), he said “kind of.” What he’s really building, he said, is a “health and wellness ecosystem” with “everything there, soup to nuts.” He didn’t put a number on how many gyms he wants, but he called the growth strategy “aggressive,” telling us that “landlords and developers who toured the Las Vegas site have offered “AAA locations at very favorable terms, with great TI” (tenant-improvement allowances that help pay for the build-out). Wahlberg’s last big bet on a gym chain might have scared off someone else. We told him we’d recently watched “ Wahl Street ,” his reality show, in which an early episode shows him getting deeply involved with the fitness chain F45 in 2019, and that we wanted to warn him about what was coming. “How did you know about the pandemic?” he joked, to laughs from the crowd. He bought into the company, known for its 45-minute classes, at a $450 million valuation. It went public in 2021, then was delisted from the NYSE in 2023 after its stock collapsed. Wahlberg said he learned a lot from the experience.

articles.title: The moral bankruptcy of Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz
articles.summary: Two of the most famous investors in Silicon Valley endorsed Donald Trump. This is less about tech generally than their investment portfolio, specifically.
articles.body_text: Last week, the founders of venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz declared their allegiance to Donald Trump in their customary fashion: talking about money on a podcast. “Sorry, Mom,” Ben Horowitz says in an episode of The Ben & Marc Show. “I know you’re going to be mad at me for this. But, like, we have to do it.” Marc Andreessen and Horowitz insist they voted for Democrats until now. They are friends with liberals. They claim to be nervous about the social blowback they will receive for this, especially because of the historically progressive nature of the tech industry and the Bay Area. But given the general movement among their class toward Trump, I think those claims about being nervous are overblown, if not performative. There is, for instance, Elon Musk’s pro-Trump super PAC, which has support from Sequoia Capital’s Shaun Maguire and 8VC’s Joe Lonsdale, among other notables. (The Wall Street Journal reported Musk is planning to donate $45 million a month, which Musk has denied.) There’s the $160 million the crypto movement has put forward in support of crypto-friendly candidates. We can’t forget their VC pal David Sacks speaking at the Republican National Convention. And last but not least, there’s Trump’s running mate choice of JD Vance, a former venture capitalist whose firm’s investors included Peter Thiel, Eric Schmidt, and Andreessen himself. This isn’t a movement. It’s a clique. The podcast itself is an extraordinary performance. At one point, Andreessen concedes that their major problems with President Joe Biden — the ones that led them to support Trump — are what most voters would consider “subsidiary” issues. “It doesn’t have anything to do with the big issues that people care about,” he says. If we take this podcast at face value, we are to believe that these subsidiary issues are the only reason they’ve chosen to endorse and donate to Trump. These subsidiary issues take precedence for Andreessen and Horowitz over, say, mass deportations and Project 2025’s attempt to end no-fault divorce. We are looking at a simple trade against personal liberty — abortion, the rights of gay and trans people, and possibly democracy itself — in favor of crypto, AI, and a tax policy they like better. For Horowitz, “probably the most emotional topic” is crypto — a16z started a $4.5 billion crypto fund in 2022, and the pair believe that the Biden administration has been deeply unfair to crypto. In Horowitz’s view, the Biden administration “basically subverted the rule of law to attack the crypto industry.” Certainly much of the crypto industry prefers Trump. But it seems obvious that there has been a lot of intra-agency squabbling as Congress dithered on passing any laws. To place the blame squarely on Biden is bizarre, particularly when we have Trump’s chaotic previous term as guidance. Sure, Trump is no longer saying Bitcoin is “a scam against the dollar,” as he did in 2021; he is scheduled to speak at the Bitcoin conference this year. But his record in office is not exactly pro-crypto. During the Trump administration, financial regulator FinCEN initially asked the public to provide comments on a crypto rule change over a 15-day period that included Christmas Eve, Christmas Day, New Year’s Eve, and New Year’s Day, which effectively shortened the comment window by four working days. There is also the Ripple Labs enforcement case, in which the SEC is seeking a $1.95 billion fine; it, too, dates to the Trump administration. The pair’s complaints about Gary Gensler, the current head of the Securities and Exchange Commission, are striking. They are particularly annoyed that he won’t pay attention to them. “We’re the largest crypto investors or largest blockchain investors in the world, and we’ve requested meetings with him at least a half a dozen times,” Horowitz says. Gensler has not met with them. Neither, they say, has Senator Elizabeth Warren or Biden himself. In fact, Andreessen makes it clear that he expects presidential attention, something he’s been getting since he was 23. Given the number of times Andreessen and Horowitz make references to various meetings with various politicians, it’s easy to get the impression that they are mostly insulted that they are being treated like ordinary constituents. From crypto, we move to AI, which Andreessen and Horowitz don’t think is being regulated correctly either. According to Horowitz, AI is as powerful as, or more powerful than, the internet and the global computer industry from the 1950s on. “This may be the biggest technological boom of all time,” Andreessen says. Andreessen says in his newsletter-cum-manifesto, “The Little Tech Agenda,” that he is worried that AI will face similar scrutiny to crypto. The FTC has issued guidance to the AI industry that indicated it will pursue companies that exaggerate what their AI can do, say they are using AI when they are not, and recklessly put products on the market without properly analyzing the risks. Meanwhile, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has told lenders that they must supply a reason for a credit denial that’s better than just “computer says no” when using AI models. These regulations have little to do with technology and a lot to do with old-fashioned lying. In the podcast, Andreessen and Horowitz single out Biden’s executive order about artificial intelligence. The order requires companies to disclose the presence of very large models, as well as to provide the government information about what the plans are for the model, what cybersecurity measures are taken to protect those models, and the results of red-team testing for sensitive subjects, among other things. This is in keeping with Horowitz’s assertion about the seriousness of the technology. So what’s the problem? The two focus on computing power. The disclosure requirements apply to “any model that was trained using a quantity of computing power greater than 1026 integer or floating-point operations, or using primarily biological sequence data and using a quantity of computing power greater than 1023 integer or floating-point operations.” Andreessen and Horowitz think specifying such a limit is ridiculous. Little tech “will be snuffed out by this kind of regulation,” Horowitz says. It is perhaps worth noting that nothing above the size specified in the executive order — the size Andreessen and Horowitz object to — even exists yet, according to Arati Prabhakar, Biden’s top tech advisor. The fundamental complaint here is that these two believe that the Biden administration’s approach to AI “enshrine[s] the two or three companies that they believe are the only companies that matter as sort of permanent monopolies,” Andreessen says. “And they’re going to just basically destroy the startup ecosystem underneath that.” Andreessen Horowitz is, of course, invested in that ecosystem, having earmarked $2.25 billion for AI applications and infrastructure. The anti-monopoly rhetoric is in keeping with a16z’s latest marketing push. According to Andreessen’s newsletter, startups are threatened by the government, which is “now far more hostile to new startups than it used to be.” Besides his objections to the way the SEC has increased its oversight of crypto, he is also upset that a stepped-up interest in antitrust has made it more difficult for him to exit investments. “Regulatory agencies are punitively blocking startups from being acquired by the same big companies the government is preferencing in so many other ways,” Andreessen writes. After all, the Federal Trade Commission has launched an inquiry into Big Tech’s partnerships and investments with startups — with the goal of seeing if those partnerships squash competition. The irony is so obvious it’s almost embarrassing to point it out. Andreessen says he is upset that Big Tech is too powerful, but he opposes antitrust action because that blocks a route for VCs to exit. Either you’re comfortable with Big Tech getting bigger, in which case acquisitions are fine, or you want little tech to be competitive, which means blocking industry consolidation. Mainly, it seems that Andreessen believes in cashing out. In the podcast, Andreessen and Horowitz pointedly name Google as a threat to startups. “Google, I think we would all agree, is more powerful than probably 95 percent of countries in the world,” Horowitz says at one point. Google, specifically, is a sore spot with the right wing. Vice presidential nominee Vance has already said it should be broken up. Vance believes Google is controlling information and skewing too far left. Of course, Google’s moderation policies don’t just apply to Google News — they also affect YouTube, which hosts a great many right-wing podcasts without issue. It’s unclear how seriously to take Andreessen and Horowitz’s complaints about Big Tech because the complaints don’t quite square with their behavior. For instance, Facebook is similarly powerful and influential, especially in AI. Andreessen sits on its board. A16z is invested in OpenAI, which has a partnership with Microsoft — and both have lobbied strenuously for more regulation around AI. It sure seems like if a16z wants to change things at those big companies, someone could simply pick up the phone. At this point in the podcast, you could squint and say maybe the concern about AI and crypto is really about technology and progress. But from those two topics, we move on to classic rich guy shit of the most tedious kind: tax reform. Andreessen says it was “the final straw for me. This is the thing that tipped me hard.” They are upset about a proposal to alter capital gains taxes. Capital gains are paid on investment assets, and they are typically paid when the investment is sold and the gains are, in industry terms, “realized.” The new Biden treasury proposal means that for people whose wealth is worth more than $100 million, any unrealized capital gains will be taxed, too. This is what has Andreessen and Horowitz in a tizzy. It means that if they own a clutch of highly valued startup shares, they will have to pay taxes on them before they cash out. This is a “very scary proposal,” Horowitz says. Startups are illiquid assets, Andreessen points out. “Startups never go up and down. They’re never overvalued,” says Horowtiz, dryly. “There’s no bubbles.” Andreessen notes that the way the value of a startup is calculated for the purposes of this proposed tax has to do with the latest round’s valuation. Historically, one of the ways that Andreessen Horowitz has approached startup investing is to inflate a company’s valuation; it is “the OG when it comes to doling out speculative startup valuations.” The new proposed tax punishes this kind of behavior — a high valuation means a high tax. “This makes startups completely implausible,” says Andreessen. “Venture capital just ends. Firms like ours don’t exist.” This is followed by an anxiety spiral that is sort of difficult to convey in text; I suggest you listen for yourself. “California is done,” says Andreessen. “It’s total destruction.” The taxes won’t just target the wealthy; they’ll come for everyone. “Once the structure gets established, the politicians do what they do: they’ll walk the numbers up,” Andreessen says. “Presto chango, we’re Argentina!” says Horowitz. Finally, Horowitz gets ahold of himself. “By the way, this one probably won’t get all the way through the system,” he says. “But it might!” There is another issue that might cause wreckage throughout Silicon Valley. It is immigration. An awful lot of immigrants comprise Silicon Valley’s talent pool — a huge swath of engineers in the US are on H-1B visas. The Trump / Vance ticket is virulently anti-immigrant. The current CEOs of Google, Microsoft, Adobe, and IBM are all immigrants. So are Peter Thiel and Elon Musk. Mark Zuckerberg and Bill Gates are involved in Fwd.us, a lobbying group dedicated to immigration reform that Musk and Sacks both left. If there were an issue that would rally the people who care most about progress, innovation, and talent, you’d think protecting the immigrants who’ve built lives and careers in tech would be it. Stopping immigration is a core issue of the Trump campaign. During the Republican National Convention, delegates held up signs saying “Mass Deportation Now.” Trump has called the H-1B, the visa many tech workers use to come to Silicon Valley, “very bad” and “unfair” to US workers. In his previous term, he targeted H-1B visa applications specifically; in the fiscal year 2018, almost 25 percent of applications were denied, up from about 13 percent the year before. In fiscal year 2019, 20 percent of H-1B applications were denied. The denials plummeted after several Trump administration rules were thrown out by courts; the denial rate in 2022 was just 2 percent. Immigration plainly matters for crypto — as Ethereum founder Vitalik Buterin says, “The crypto industry is uniquely international, and so immigration law is crypto law.” Buterin is one of the most influential voices in crypto, and Ethereum is the foundation for a swath of Andreessen Horowitz’s investment portfolio. Among the investments that rely on it are MakerDAO, VeeFriends, Dapper Labs, and EigenLayer. It is remarkable that the founder of Ethereum is saying that voting for Trump is against the crypto ethos, and the big crypto investors are doing it anyway. The word “immigration” is only mentioned by Andreessen and Horowitz in the podcast when they discuss the rally in which someone attempted an assassination: Trump had turned his head to look at a chart that purported to show illegal immigration into the US as the bullet whizzed by. I wondered why such an important issue for tech wasn’t addressed, so I emailed Margit Wennmachers, a16z’s PR guru, to ask. She didn’t reply. After I finished listening to the podcast, a few things kept nagging at me. Take the very beginning of the podcast. Once upon a time, Andreessen says, you could get very rich and then give the money away in philanthropy, “and you get enormous credit for that. And, you know, it absolves you of whatever.” At some point in the last 10 years, some people suggested that maybe rich people should pay more taxes instead of giving their money away — that perhaps the whims of some random rich person are not the best way to support the most vulnerable in our society. Andreessen and Horowitz suggest that this critique of philanthropy is simply jealousy. It also unbalanced “the deal.” “The deal,” as described on the podcast, is vague. To my ear, it sounds like this: Tech companies could basically do whatever they wanted, as long as people who worked there paid high taxes and donated enough money to charitable causes. The money — taxes, donations — made them the good guys. Andreessen and Horowitz point to the mid-2010s — that is, the era of low interest rates — as the time of “the deal” unraveling. Notably, this is around the time that the tech hype cycle became obvious even to people who weren’t paying attention. This year, it’s scooters! Now it’s viral media companies! Now it’s metaverse! Now it’s crypto! Now it’s AI! These ideas were more or less rejected by the market, except possibly AI. The one thing all these hype cycles had in common was VCs talking their books, as publicly as possible. That charge was led by Andreessen Horowitz. So now, instead of investing in things the market wants, Andreessen and Horowitz appear to be gambling on legislation instead. Their timing is remarkable; not even a week after their Trump endorsement, Biden dropped out of the race, rallying the Democrats behind Vice President Kamala Harris. In the hours immediately following the announcement, small-money donors raised $46.7 million for her campaign. By endorsing Trump, Andreessen and Horowitz have effectively lost whatever leverage they might have had with the Harris campaign. But maybe that doesn’t matter. Near the end of the podcast, Horowitz says that he was shaken by the assassination attempt on Donald Trump because he’s friends with Ivanka, his daughter, and Jared Kushner, his son-in-law. “Ivanka and the kids were just at my house,” Horowitz says, of learning Trump was shot. “We went to see David Copperfield and all that. So my brain was almost frozen because I had this feeling about, ‘Oh my god, Grandpa just got shot.’” As for Andreessen, he has been inveighing against “woke” capital, engaging in Twitter culture wars, and complaining about what he views as the media’s hostility to free speech for a while now. In Andreessen’s 2023 “Techno-Optimist Manifesto,” he lists what he terms “patron saints” of the movement. They include Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, an Italian futurist who was also the co-author of The Fascist Manifesto; Nick Land, whose writing is a foundational text for the so-called alt-right; Neven Sesardic, a philosopher who argues that race is biologically real and not socially constructed; and Vilfredo Pareto, who argued that democracy is an illusion. And this talk about democracy brings me to Curtis Yarvin, personal friend of vice presidential candidate Vance. Yarvin, a software developer, is openly anti-democracy. (Yarvin’s recent newsletter, in response to Biden dropping out, enthusiastically advocates for a return to monarchy. Freak shit.) One of Yarvin’s ideas, called “retire all government employees” or RAGE, is part of Project 2025, a Heritage Foundation proposal for what Trump should do if he wins. This rhetoric was echoed by Vance in 2021, who called out Yarvin by name. So this VC cabal is trading against the basic principles of America — not merely against personal freedom, but democracy itself — in the hopes of profit. It’s not the first time tech has made the trade against freedom; IBM made it during the Holocaust. In venture capital, you are what you fund. Andreessen and Horowitz understand this, even embody it. But they aren’t just funding the issues they discuss on their podcast; they are funding Trump and Vance. That means those donations are anti-abortion, anti-immigration, and possibly even anti-democracy because that is what the Trump / Vance ticket stands for. These are not subsidiary issues: these are now what two of Silicon Valley’s most prominent figures now stand for, too. Is that a good investment? Correction July 24: An earlier version of this article misstated the donation strategy of a crypto super PAC. The group also spends money on Democratic candidates, not just right-wing ones.

articles.title: Lyx-plundrarna – mitt i jättekaoset
articles.summary: Många lyxbutiker plundras under kravallerna i Frankrike. ”Det är rena apokalypsen”, säger en butiksägare.
articles.body_text: Många lyxbutiker plundras under kravallerna i Frankrike. – Det är rena apokalypsen, säger en butiksägare. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Över 2 000 personer har gripits i samband med de omfattande protesterna i Frankrike . Men oroligheterna har också lett till att märken som Galeries Lafayette, Ralph Lauren, Gucci, Louis Vuitton, Hermès, Versace, Apple och Christian Dior har fått sina butiker plundrade i PAris, Marseille och andra städer. En man som varit butiksägare i centrala Paris i 30 år sade att de maskerade vandalerna ”krossar allt runtomkring oss”. – De har förstört min verksamhet och krossat mina skyltfönster. De tar glasskärvor för att kasta på kravallpolisen. De ger oss fingret och säger att de ska skära halsen av oss. Det är rena apokalypsen, säger han till radiostationen RTL. ”Våra Lacoste- och Aigle-butiker plundras, liksom så många andra företag runtom i Frankrike”, skriver Lacoste-vd:n Thierry Guibert på Instagram. Parisbon Cecile Rogue sade att ”grupper av ungdomar plundrade och slog sönder allt”. – Det är fruktansvärt och skrämmande, säger Rogue. Lyons borgmästare Gregory Doucet beskrev helgens kaos i staden som ”avskyvärt”. I ett tv-sänt tal till nationen på söndagen betonade Frankrikes president Emmanuel Macron att det finns en tydlig skillnad mellan personer som ”demonstrerade med legitima krav” och ”de som förstör, krossar och plundrar”. – De kommer att ställas till svars, säger Macron.

articles.title: Putins plan – göra upp med dem om kriget
articles.summary: Putin vill hålla ett toppmöte med Trump och Xi – men utan Zelenskyj – för att diskutera ett Ukraina-avtal. Det uppger källor för Wall Street Journal.
articles.body_text: Putin vill hålla ett toppmöte med Trump och Xi för att diskutera ett Ukraina-avtal – men Zelenskyj är inte inbjuden. Det uppger källor för Wall Street Journal . Tidningen skriver att ett sånt möte ”skulle få varningsklockorna att ringa i Europas huvudstäder”. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Ryske presidenten Vladimir Putin Putin föreslår ett toppmöte med USA:s president Donald Trump och Kinas president Xi Jinping för att diskutera en uppgörelse om Ukraina. Putin lade fram förslaget i ett telefonsamtal med Donald Trump för knappt två veckor sedan, enligt tidningen. Den ryske ledarens tanke är att Putin, Trump och Xi skulle möta varandra nästa månad i ett försök att förhandla fram ett slut på det fyra år långa kriget ”på ett sätt som skulle gynna Moskva”, enligt personer med insyn i diskussionerna. Ukrainas president Volodymyr Zelenskyj skulle inte bli inbjuden i samtalen, enligt källorna. Kremls talesperson Dmitrij Peskov bekräftar att diskussioner om ett potentiellt möte mellan de tre ledarna pågår. – Det finns ännu ingen klar bild av hur själva mötet skulle se ut eller vilka frågor som skulle stå på dagordningen, även om alla tre parter är införstådda med att ett sådant möte hypotetiskt sett skulle kunna äga rum, säger Putins talesperson Dmitrij Peskov till tidningen. Ett sådant toppmöte ”skulle vara utan motstycke och få varningsklockorna att ringa i Europas huvudstäder och på andra håll”, enligt tidningen. Detta är en nyhetsartikel. articles.title: Obama om Trump: ”Vidrigt”
articles.summary: Donald Trump försöker få kongressledamoten Ilhan Omar, en av hans hårdaste kritiker, utkastad ur USA enligt ex-presidenten Barack Obama: ”Det är vidrigt.”
articles.body_text: Donald Trump försöker få kongressledamoten Ilhan Omar, en av hans hårdaste kritiker, utkastad ur USA enligt ex-presidenten Barack Obama. Han anser att Trumps agerande ”borde uppröra alla”, skriver MSNOW . Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Ilhan Omar kom till USA från Somalia som tolvåring. Fem år senare blev hon naturaliserad amerikansk medborgare. Numera är hon demokratisk representanthusledamot. ”Där har hon varit en av Trump-administrationens hårdaste kritiker, vilket har lett till att presidenten upprepade gånger pekat ut henne som någon som han anser inte hör hemma i landet”, skriver Barack Obama, president mellan 2009 och 2017, på X . Nyligen gjorde federala agenter en razzia i Omars hem i Washington DC och konfiskerade hennes bärbara dator, mobiltelefon, pass samt dokument med koppling till hennes och familjens immigration. ”Det är en grundläggande princip i amerikansk demokrati att regeringen inte kan selektivt rikta in sig på individer enbart på grund av deras politiska övertygelser eller vad de säger. Men det är precis vad Trump-administrationen gör mot kongressledamoten Ilhan Omar”, skriver Obama. Detta har resulterat i att ”Omars liv har vänts upp och ner”, enligt Obama. Han uppger att Trump-administrationen aktivt försöker utvisa Omar och beskriver dess agerande som ”vidrigt”. ”Den federala regeringens fulla tyngd läggs på en laglydig folkvald tjänsteman eftersom hon har vågat kritisera presidenten. Och det är inte första gången detta har hänt. Under president Trump har justitiedepartementet upprepade gånger gått till angrepp mot dem han anser vara sina politiska fiender”, skriver Obama. Trump har kallat Omar för ”skräp”, enligt MSNOW. Vicepresident JD Vance hävdade i mars, utan att lägga fram bevis för det, att Omar ”definitivt begick immigrationsbedrägeri”. ”Det faktum att en president och hans administration är villig att genomföra sådana uppenbara försök att skrämma någon borde uppröra alla amerikaner”, skriver Obama. articles.summary: Leila Ben Salem var med på ett jobbmöte. Då blev 45-åringen attackerad och mördad. Kanadas premiärminister har fördömt ”det skamliga brottet”.
articles.body_text: Leila Ben Salem var med på ett jobbmöte. Då blev 45-åringen attackerad och mördad. Kanadas premiärminister har fördömt ”det skamliga brottet”, skriver Montreal Gazette . Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Leila Ben Salem arbetade vid Kanadas skattemyndighet. Hon deltog i ett videomöte med jobbet den 22 september när hon attackerades i sin lägenhet i Montreal. Polisen fann Salem livlös i bostaden. Den 45-åriga kvinnan dödförklarades på platsen, enligt CBC. Dagar efter att Salem hittades död framförde Kanadas premiärminister Mark Carney sina ”djupaste kondoleanser till hennes familj, anhöriga och kolleger”. – Fru Ben Salem var en värderad medlem av Kanadas skattemyndighet, engagerad i att stå kanadensarna till tjänst, vilket hon gjorde vid tidpunkten för överfallet, sade Carney. Premiärministern utlovade att regeringen skulle göra allt för att säkerställa att ”gärningsmannen ställs till svars för detta skamliga brott och får sitt rättmätiga straff”. En 33-årig man åtalades i helgen för mordet på Salem. Mordmotivet är fortfarande oklart, men polisen uppgav att Salems död inte var relaterad till våld i en nära relation. Detta är en nyhetsartikel. articles.title: Beskedet: Så började dödliga katastrofen
articles.summary: Fyra personer dog och 39 skadades i brandkatastrofen på en militärbas i Kanada. Nu framkommer nya uppgifter om vad som hände under den ödedigra övningen.
articles.body_text: Fyra personer har dött och 39 har skadats i brandkatastrofen på en militärbas i Kanada. Nu framkommer nya uppgifter om vad som hände under den ödedigra övningen. – Det är inte normalt att en brand sprider sig så snabbt, säger generalmajor Wade Rutland. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Det var strax efter klockan 16 på lördagen, lokal tid, som polis och räddningstjänst larmades om en brand i ett övningsområde på militärbasen Wainwright i kanadensiska Alberta. En omfattande insats pågick i tio timmar innan branden kunde bringas under kontroll. De skadade fördes till fyra olika sjukhus i provinsen, där sjukvården tvingades aktivera särskilda katastrofrutiner. På söndagskvällen bekräftade Kanadas premiärminister Mark Carney att fyra soldater omkommit. Därtill har 39 personer skadats, varav 19 uppges vara i kritiskt tillstånd. Branden beskrivs som den värsta tragedin som drabbat landets militär under fredstid. Omständigheterna kring händelsen har hittills varit oklara, men nu berättar generalmajor Wade Rutland att branden började när gräs i övningsområdet fattade eld. Branden befann sig först flera kilometer bort, men ”ovanligt starka vindar” fick elden att snabbt sprida sig mot en skjutbana där flera övningar med skarp ammunition pågick. – De kastade handgranater och genomförde vad vi kallar en sektionsattack, där tio soldater attackerade en simulerad fiende, säger Rutland på en pressträff. Enligt generalmajoren hade väderförhållandena under större delen av dagen legat inom gränserna för militärens säkerhetsrutiner. – Det är inte normalt att en brand sprider sig så snabbt, säger Rutland.

articles.summary: Jasmine Gill försvann. Maken hävdade att ICE hade gripit frun. Sedan avslöjades hans lögn och ett makabert fynd gjordes.
articles.body_text: Sedan avslöjades hans lögn och ett makabert fynd gjordes, skriver People . Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Polisens misstankar riktades snart mot Jasmines make Gurinder Gill, 28. articles.title: Kungen ”rasande” – efter vanlig gest
articles.summary: Hovreportern Trine Larsen gjorde en vanlig gest när hon träffade kung Fredrik och hans familj. ”Han blir rasande”, säger Larsen. Sen fick hon förklaringen.
articles.body_text: Hovreportern Trine Larsen gjorde en helt vanlig gest när hon träffade kung Fredrik och hans familj. – Han blir rasande, säger Larsen till danska B.T. Sedan fick hon förklaringen till kunglighetens ilska. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Hovreportern Trine Larsen har följt den danska kungafamiljen i över 30 år. Hon är aktuell med kommande boken ”Hovreportern” om sina möten med kungafamiljen. Larsen berättar för B.T. om en händelse när hon träffade dåvarande kronprins, sedermera kung, Frederik en vintermorgon i Schweiz för flera år sedan. Frederik var på skidsemester med frun Mary och barnen Christian, Isabella, Vincent och Josephine som då var små. Medan Frederik hjälpte Isabella med sina skidor hälsade Larsen på dem. – Vi säger: ”God morgon, Ers Höghet.” Och så tittar han upp och blir rasande. Sedan säger han bara: ”Jag bryr mig inte ett dugg om det här. Om ni tror att jag kandiderar för någonting så har ni fel”, säger Larsen. – Jag tänkte: ”Vad händer här?” Det hade gått några månader sedan jag pratade med honom senast, och inget hade hänt sedan dess. Jag blev väldigt förvånad. Det var helt okej om han hade något emot det, men då kunde han ha sagt det på ett bättre sätt, säger Larsen. Hon kontaktade hovets dåvarande kommunikationschef Lene Balleby och berättade om mötet med Frederik i skidbacken. Kort därefter blev Larsen uppringd av Balleby som bad henne att träffa den dåvarande kronprinsen på en restaurang i närheten. – Han kommer gående mot oss och ropar så högt att alla kan höra det: ”Trine Larsen, jag hör dig säga att jag är arg. Jag är inte arg alls”, säger Larsen med ett leende. Sedan förklarade han orsaken till sin irritation i skidbacken. – Hans ord var: ”Hur skulle du själv ha reagerat om du skulle ut tidigt med barn som vill åka skidor medan du inte har sovit hela natten för att tvillingarna gråter?”, säger Larsen som anser att ”alla föräldrar kan känna igen sig i en sådan situation”.

articles.title: Trumps förslag för fred – pekar ut ryska gasen • Rådet till Europa: Köp mer
articles.summary: Donald Trump gör dieselaffärer med Vladimir Putin. Nu uppmanar Trumpadministrationen länder i Europa att börja köpa rysk gas igen, skriver New York Times.
articles.body_text: Donald Trump gör dieselaffärer med Vladimir Putin. Nu uppmanar Trumpadministrationen länder i Europa att börja köpa rysk gas igen, skriver New York Times. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Donald Trump och Vladimir Putin enades tidigare i oktober om att Ryssland ska släppa ett par miljoner ton diesel till den amerikanska marknaden och världsmarknaden under de närmaste månaderna. Samtidigt stoppar den amerikanske presidenten nya sanktioner mot Ryssland. Dieselavtalet och Trumps u-sväng om sanktionerna har fått stenhård kritik. Men Trump tror att mer handel med Ryssland kan motivera Putin att vilja sluta fred. New York Times rapporterar att Trumpadministrationen föreslår att Europa återupptar inköpen av större mängder rysk gas. Trumps fredsförhandlare, Steve Witkoff och Jared Kushner, ska ha tagit upp idén i diskussioner med europeiska och ukrainska företrädare, enligt personer med insyn i samtalen. Tidningen skriver vidare att de amerikanska förhandlarna har uppmanat Ukraina att överväga att öppna de gasledningar som tidigare transporterade rysk fossilgas till Europa. De har påpekat att en del av intäkterna skulle tillfalla landet i form av transitavgifter, samtidigt som miljontals européer skulle få tillgång till billigare energi. Vita huset skriver i ett uttalande till New York Times att kriget ”driver upp energipriserna i hela Europa” och att det orsakar ”betydande ekonomiska svårigheter i både Ryssland och Ukraina”. ”USA har arbetat nära Ukraina och våra europeiska partner med ett omfattande fredsförslag som innehåller ekonomiska incitament för både Ryssland och Ukraina som en del av en slutlig uppgörelse. Vårt mål är inte bara att få slut på striderna, utan att skapa förutsättningar för varaktig fred, ekonomisk återhämtning och ökad stabilitet i hela regionen”. Enligt New York Times källor har flera europeiska företrädare som deltagit i samtalen reagerat mycket negativt på förslaget. Det går dessutom rakt emot EU:s beslut om att fasa ut rysk gas till hösten 2027. Vissa europeiska regeringar menar att det amerikanska förslaget skulle stärka populistiska krafter, som AfD i Tyskland, som vill se en ökad import av rysk gas och olja. Dessutom räknar vissa europeiska och ukrainska företrädare, enligt tidningens källor, med att USA skulle försöka skaffa sig ägarandelar så att staten eller amerikanska företag får del av vinsterna.
